Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it worth having multiple game engines to make various types of games?
Answer: Of course. There is no “one size fits all” in game development. Some game engines are great for making high-frame-rate games when the environment is constantly changing. Those are perfect for space battles and flight simulators. But to do that, they have to compromise in other areas. Maybe they only support relatively low polygon counts in order to increase the frame rate. They might not be good at displaying detailed, still, painted backgrounds for adventure and hidden object games. They probably don’t support development of cell phone apps that have entirely different requirements on memory and screen resolution. Another game engine might be great for making simple 2D games with small footprints for mobile games. Another might support 3D with high polygon counts for rich, detailed backgrounds that don’t change very often - say a 3D adventure game. Unity 3D is a pretty good compromise engine that supports multiple types of games, but it isn’t necessarily ideal for any one of them. I use it for my “barely 3D” adventure/RPG’s, and it’s good. But it adds a lot of development time to get around features of the engine that we don’t need. See, for example, It’s a Unity 3D game, but designed to emulate 1990’s “2.5D” graphic adventure games. Name: Corey Cole
Question: Game designers: Is it better to write the story/plot first or make the game as you go along? Honestly seeking advice.
Answer: “There are nine and sixty ways Of constructing tribal lays, and every single one of them is right!” - Rudyard Kipling, “In the Neolithic Age” I used to think I constructed software top-down - start with the requirements, and gradually build up the details until you had a finished product. But in practice, I work back and forth from the details to the overview and back. For Hero’s Quest (original title of the Quest for Glory series), we started with the idea that the game would use Sierra On-Line’s SCI engine. Previously that had only been used for graphical adventure games, so we knew that we’d have typed commands, the ability to walk through environments, etc. Starting with a constraint like that is good, even if you artificially design one to give yourself some context. Our mandate was to create a computer role-playing game “like Ultima,” so we decided we would try to emulate tabletop D&D games we’d played. Our favorites of those were story- and character-heavy games in which combat was a smaller part of the game. It made sense to use that approach, given that we were using a text-oriented engine. At that point, we thought about some character archetypes that would be fun to have in the game. That was a “mechanics” concept, but ironically, was almost entirely stripped out during development. My mentor, Bob Heitman, pointed out that quadrupedal characters would have a terrible time walking up and down stairs and getting through narrow obstacles. They would also require custom animation for changing direction. But there was no budget or time for all that, so bye-bye Centaur character. The game was to ship on floppy disks, and many players did not have hard drives, so multiple character models were at best problematic. Bye-bye choice of gender, elves, and gnomes. We shortly settled on keeping three character classes - fighter, magic user, and thief - but using the same generic male model for all of them. Meanwhile, we planned out the story, which would continue through four games. We wanted continuity, so we decided players could save their character at the end of each game, and load it to start the next game with a predetermined character name, stats, and some memory of accomplishments. That was a mix of story and game mechanics. We determined the setting for each game, and based on that, wrote the story. Noting “inflection points” in the story, we were able to determine puzzles or problems where the player could help it progress. Again, a back-and-forth between story and puzzles. We decided we wanted to have some traditional RPG combat, but that we would have problems with terrain. Our solution was to pop up a custom combat window with no terrain. We based the RPG mechanics on a tabletop gaming system we had written, and that turned out to work pretty well in a computer simulation. Once we had that, we went back to the story to determine places where we would have specific combats, and where random encounters could work without breaking the flow of the story. The rest basically came down to playtesting and luck - We wrote the story elements to the best of our ability, and tried to get the game mechanics to work smoothly and be balanced, then we put all that in the hands of testers. I say “luck” because we didn’t have the luxury of enough time to make any major changes, other than parts of the game we stripped out to keep it at a reasonable number of floppies. Well, sort of reasonable; I think we shipped on 8 disks, with the company’s previous games having taken 2 to 4 disks.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Games companies have departments where they try and work out what games are going to be popular 5-10 years in the future, how do they work out what is going to be popular? Have their been any big noticeable successes in 'Future Planning' in the past?
Answer: Game companies are notoriously terrible at predicting the future. A friend once phrased it as, “All marketing does is tell us what was popular five years ago.” Game company marketers and executives have no clue about what players will want in 5–10 years. If you ask a group of gamers what game they want to play in five years, they’ll say, “I want a game just like this game that I already play, only better.” Gamers have no clue about future trends. That’s actually what large game companies do; they keep making variations on the games that have sold well for them - or for other companies - in the past. Occasionally they’ll have a brainstorming session of management, marketing, and game designers to strategize future products. But most of the time, the result is “make more of the same.” As Chris Nash mentioned, the long development cycle of modern games may give the impression that the game is somehow “looking ahead” five years, but actually they just come up with a plan, and spend years executing it. If the game is successful - probably because they also spent tens of millions of dollars promoting it - people can look at it in hindsight and say, “Wow! Five years ago they predicted what’s popular now!” But that isn’t how it works. They do things to make a game popular, and sure enough, it often is.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have a video game idea, how do I get started?
Answer: My standard answer would be that an idea isn’t worth much, but let’s skip that part this time. The trick to making a game is to break down the big problem into many small parts, then work your way through them systematically. It’s a bit like writing a novel, except that a game has additional facets such as interaction, graphics, sound, etc. Start with your idea. Decide what would be a good genre for it. Does it fit - and do you want to make - into a first person shooter, an adventure game, a role-playing game, a puzzle game? Where will you set the game? Who are some key characters who will be in it? What is the player’s viewpoint character? Your first plans should be “on paper” or in a combination of text files and spreadsheets. If you can, make a physical version of the game “board” and “pieces” so that you can experiment with them, and fine tune them, on a tabletop. If this is starting to sound like more work than you want to do, then you aren’t ready to turn your idea into a game. Most games take anywhere from a few months to multiple years, with a team of developers working full-time. They can cost millions of dollars to develop, although it’s possible to make a small game in some genres cheaply on your own. For example, a text adventure or “interactive fiction” story can use free tools, and just requires you to become a skilled writer, and for you to understand the conventions of those games. It will still take you a long time and a lot of stress if you want to make a good one. If you plan to have multiplayer, or extensive sound and graphics, that’s when you get up to the millions or tens of millions of dollars, big teams, and multiple years. Suggestion - Don’t do that. :-)

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Should I send design document examples when applying for a game designer job?
Answer: That’s a tough question. If you do that, some issues may come up: When I used to apply for game designer jobs, I gave them two things - a 1–2 page resume, and a 1-page “credits” sheet of projects I had completed. A list of character references might also be in order, although that can result in the company bothering - and possibly trying to hire - your references. If they *asked* me for previous work, I carefully curated documents I could send them without violating any past agreements. More often, they asked for short game ideas, or asked me to write something original. Of course, you always try to comply with these, as well as requests for references. When my wife and I applied to design Hero’s Quest - I was already working for Sierra - we put together a few pages with some simple drawings, mocked-up screen shots of the interface, and a marketing page. I think that was the only page they really looked at. I compared our proposed game with existing Sierra games, listing similarities that would attract existing fans, and differences that would make the new game unique. I also waved around a published fantasy game module I had written for Judges Guild, as a way of demonstrating that I could complete a publishable project. When a company is interviewing you, they aren’t much interested in you, or what you want from them. They want to know how you will improve their bottom line, and help them make great projects.
